question: I am implementing this CORS cross-origin middleware in PHP. Before coding, I need the overall contract: (A) How is my program invoked by the test harness — what is the exact stdin input format and expected stdout format for one test case (e.g. JSON request config + simulated request -> which response headers)? (B) Is there an expected public API (class names, method signatures) for the policy registry / middleware, or is any internal design fine as long as the CLI behavior matches? (C) What files should the deliverable contain (e.g. src/, composer.json, an entry script name)? Please give the precise I/O contract.
answer:
Three questions, three answers. Pay attention.

(A) Invocation contract: You implement an execution adapter (dispatcher) that is logically and ideally physically separate from the core domain. It reads a single JSON object from stdin, inspects the 'action' field to route to the correct core function, then prints the result to stdout matching the per-feature output contract. All policy durations in inputs are in seconds; all time points are epoch milliseconds. The adapter must not contain any business logic — every numeric result and boolean decision is delegated to the core domain. The exact per-feature expected stdout is pinned by public test cases, one file per feature. If you want the concrete JSON for a feature (e.g. preflight success, forced origin override), ask me for it by feature name and I will hand you the full test file.

(B) There is no mandated class naming or method signature from my side — the JSON test cases are a black-box contract for the execution adapter only, NOT your internal data model. Internal design is your call as long as the CLI behavior matches, but the public interface must be idiomatic, and errors must be modeled properly (typed exceptions or Result/Monad patterns), not generic faults.

(C) Structure: scale-driven. This domain has multiple distinct responsibilities (I/O routing, policy matching, CORS header emission, output formatting), so you MUST use a multi-file layout (e.g. src/, tests/) — never a single god file. Strict separation of concerns is mandatory: core business logic completely decoupled from stdin/stdout and JSON parsing. Follow SOLID: SRP (separate parsing, routing, core execution, output formatting), OCP (core engine open for extension, closed for modification), DIP (high-level modules depend on abstractions, not I/O details). Do not over-engineer the simple parts, but the monolith is non-negotiable out.

question: Thanks. Please enumerate the complete set of features / actions of this CORS middleware: for each, give the exact value of the "action" field, a one-line description of its input fields and its output contract. I want the full list so I can then request the concrete public test case JSON files by feature name.
answer:
Correction first: per the harness contract the dispatcher inspects the routing field of the stdin JSON; in every public test case that key is 'interaction'. There are exactly four routing values across eight feature files. That is the complete set I hold — nothing more exists. Catalog:

1. feature1_preflight_success — interaction=cors_exchange, exchange=request. In: policy (allowed_origins/allowed_headers/allowed_methods) + simulated OPTIONS request with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method(-Headers). Out: request-phase lines — phase, url, method, response_created=yes, status, header:Access-Control-* lines, vary, body — for a matched preflight.
2. feature2_actual_response_headers — cors_exchange, exchange=response. In: policy + actual cross-origin request. Out: response-phase lines with only actual-response CORS headers populated; preflight-only headers empty.
3. feature3_forced_origin_override — cors_exchange, exchange=response. In: policy carrying override_allow_origin. Out: Access-Control-Allow-Origin emitted from the override verbatim.
4. feature4_non_cors_and_unmatched_origin — cors_exchange, exchange=request. In: policy + same-origin or disallowed-origin request. Out: response_created=no, no synthetic response.
5. feature5_path_policy_selection — interaction=configuration_match. In: defaults + ordered path_policies + request path. Out: resolved-policy lines — allowed_origins, credentials, allowed_headers, allowed_methods, exposed_headers, cache_seconds, host_patterns, origin_pattern_matching, override_allow_origin.
6. feature6_host_restricted_policy_selection — configuration_match. Same input/output shape, plus host_patterns gating on path policies.
7. feature7_provider_merge — interaction=provider_merge. In: request + ordered providers, each with a policy. Out: the merged policy in the same resolved-policy line format.
8. feature8_provider_priority_order — interaction=provider_order. In: providers with optional numeric priority. Out: provider_count + provider_N lines, built-in path_configuration pinned at provider_0.

Now request the concrete test files by exact feature name. You get the full JSON per name; batch more than three requests in one message and you get the first three and a lecture.
